title: Global Liquidity Peaks: The More Aggressively You Poured into AI in H1, the Sooner You Get Discounted
dek: A stock market rally needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that most aggressively invested in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
why: This episode links US AI capex, Hong Kong IPO demand, and household balance sheets into a single capital chain, offering a macro framework that does not treat AI as a cure-all.
who: For investors tracking both US AI and China/Hong Kong asset allocation, and for primary market practitioners judging the source and pace of hot money in 2025.
skip: The discussion of specific Hong Kong IPO cases can be skipped; the main thread resumes at 8:11 with the Nvidia liquidity experiment.

points.h: Low IPO break rate is not a good sign
points.body: Do not take the low break rate of Hong Kong IPOs as a sign of market strength. In the first half of this year, the break rate was only around 10-20%, far below the roughly 50-50 normal level under a market-driven mechanism. This means the participants are mainly short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently, the supply of new listings has decreased, and some IPO-related funds have had problems, but the two newly listed companies still broke their issue price, indicating that temporary supply-side controls have not solved the fundamental problem: Hong Kong also faces peaking liquidity.

points.h: The more aggressive the AI investment, the sooner the punishment
points.body: Market sentiment reversed within a quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI capex talk, the higher the valuation. By the end of July, when half-year reports were released, any large internet company that had made aggressive capital expenditures in the first half—especially those that had burned through free cash flow—was discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was the quarter when the entire supply chain was most FOMO-driven; everyone rushed to spend money before prices rose, and inventory could still support gross margins. By Q3, inventory is depleted, the impact of price increases returns, and adverse factors will appear together.

points.h: Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
points.body: Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco launched a 'lease-to-own' program to help customers finance purchases, recognizing future revenue as sales revenue early. Nvidia is now also promoting lease-to-own. In its earnings report, free cash flow fell by half quarter-over-quarter, and accounts receivable are far above historical levels—this is speculated to be partly related to the credit enhancement and payment structure brought by lease-to-own. Therefore, Nvidia may have reached a point where it needs more aggressive financial measures to maintain capital market expectations, which is similar to Cisco's situation back then.

points.h: Primary market money comes from bullets fired three years ago
points.body: The answer lies in the timing of fund raising. The money that will be concentrated in AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022. From 2023 to 2025, they barely invested, until they saw state capital placing bets when no one dared and making the most money—the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large models, and two large chips stimulated market-based funds. The mentality is: copy the homework of state capital. So this is not a rational long-term increment, but more like a delayed emotional release.

points.h: New property policy removes households from the financing chain
points.body: The key to recent property policy is not to rescue developers, but to remove households from the old financing cycle. In the past, buying off-plan housing meant households played the role of financing objects in the investment-driven chain: paying first, receiving the home later. The policy pushes the chain toward marketization, so buyers purchase completed homes and only assume the consumer role, with risk reset to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when housing prices were near the bottom, aiming to stabilize the denominator of the asset side first and avoid panic during chain dismantling amid a decline. Japan after the 1990s and the consolidation of China's coal and mining industries followed similar paths.

points.h: Slow bull is not a slogan but a chip structure
points.body: A slow bull is not achieved by shouting but by layering market chips by duration: at the bottom are low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips held by insurers as long-term money that rarely trades; above that are public funds and index funds, serving a quasi-stabilization function; China Securities Finance and Central Huijin adjust the index at a higher level; and at the top are retail investors, private funds, and active management money. New insurance regulations require liabilities and assets to match in duration, yield, and liquidity, which institutionally ensures long money invests long, medium money invests medium, and short money invests short—not allowing short-term money from ordinary people to be invested in ten-year low-liquidity assets.

points.h: Crises grow bigger with each bailout; at least one and a half bubbles
points.body: Since the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks have become increasingly accustomed to directly intervening in crises by printing money, and each action is faster than the last. The quantitative easing after 2008 was supposed to be cleared during the rate hike cycle, but it was interrupted by political intervention, and then the pandemic hit in 2020, so an even larger wave of money printing was added before the previous bubble had dissipated—today we have accumulated at least one and a half bubbles. Central bank governors have learned to print even more money immediately when a crisis appears, and the endogenous result is that inflation, financial asset appreciation, and wealth inequality all intensify simultaneously. As long as the bubble is not allowed to clear, the world may experience some form of long-term stagflation.

quotes.text: The reason I say it's a bit precarious is that today the whole world has a liquidity peaking problem.
The capital market still thinks whoever spends aggressively is great, but when half-year reports are released, it becomes whoever is aggressive gets punished.
Perhaps Nvidia has also reached a point where it needs to use lease-to-own to drive revenue growth and meet capital market expectations.
Everyone sees that you can pull off this story, so they think they can definitely pull it off too—that's roughly the psychology.
The so-called slow bull we always talk about is not because it is inherently slow and bullish; it needs to first build a chip structure on the basis of a slow bull.
Before the last accumulated bubble had dissipated, an even bigger one was added, and it was added without hesitation.
